chapter_title: Concerning the Fifty Lord's Days; to what Mysteries do they correspond? Or the Second (Fifty); to whose Sign (are they)?
chapter_note: The chapter opens with a formal Q&A frame about institutional fasting (catechumens/elect). The oldest layer appears chiefly in ¶2–¶4 as a numerical-cosmological exposition (five garments × five powers → twenty-five limbs/sons; ascent of the Summons/Answer/Obedience; living food). The second half (¶5–¶8) drifts strongly into institutional legitimation and then explicitly NT/apostolic exempla (apostles, Christ’s temptation, Simon the leper, tomb), matching the chapter’s high editorial-fatigue signal.

paragraphs.temporal_note: Hagiographic/dialogue frame with disciple-question formula (‘I beseech you, my master’), plus explicit institutional categories (catechumens/elect) anchoring the topic in community practice rather than cosmic mechanism.

paragraphs.core_text: Happen you know that [in eac]h one of these five garments that the [First] Man summoned there are five powers. They shall be counted to the [ ... each] other, these five, and five times [ ... ] their number. However, at the time [ ... ] the Summons went down. The Answer wished to ascend with it. And the Summons with the Obedience [constitute] twenty-five characteristics in their twenty-five limbs, [which] are the sons of the Man. The Summons and [the Obed]ience were raised to the heights through them.
paragraphs.removed_material: Removed dialogue attribution/opening frame clause: “Then [he] says to his questioner and they with him:”. This is a compilation-layer speech tag.
paragraphs.temporal_note: Core substrate shows systematic numbered correspondences (five garments × five powers; twenty-five limbs/sons) and impersonal cosmological mechanics (descent/ascent of Summons/Answer/Obedience). The only later material is the brief speech-attribution wrapper.

paragraphs.core_text: Just as their fa[ther] the Living Man raised himself up through them, by these these other ones have set up all things a[bov]e and below. Indeed, these are what are called pentecost, the fifty great days. They fasted from their [foo]d, [w]hich is their own.
paragraphs.removed_material: Removed liturgical/institutional linkage embedded in the sentence: “that are the [archetypes of the] holy [d]ays” (cosmos → church calendar application).
paragraphs.temporal_note: Begins in a cosmological register (Living Man; cosmic ‘setting up’ above/below) but then is used to ground ‘holy days’ terminology; the excised clause is an editorial move from cosmic description to institutional calendrics.

paragraphs.core_text: So, from that time until [the time] of [the adv]ent of Jesus the Splendour, the glorious one who came [ ... / ... t]heir food which is the [ ... ] of sou[l], which is the Summons and the Obedience [ ... ] that spiritual food. They rele[ased ... ] all these fifty days, which [ ... ] this living food suffices for all of them. It filled them all with power and richness and life. Light [ ... ] this living food that [ ... ] became rich.
paragraphs.temporal_note: Sustained cosmological exposition: ‘food’ is defined internally as the Summons/Obedience (cosmic agencies), and the effects are described as power/richness/life—mechanics within the Light-world economy, not institutional regulation.

Moves from cosmological counting to institutional calendrics and practice (‘one hundred holy days’, ‘elect fast’), using the mysteries as justification for community observance—cosmos → church application.

Explicitly legitimates the fasts via other ‘sects’ and apostolic precedent (‘apostles themselves fasted… revealed them to their disciples’). This is Christian/apostolic overlay language entering via post-NT ecclesial tradition.
Direct NT narrative exempla: Christ tempted by the devil, Simon the leper, three days in the sepulchre—material that enters the Kephalaia through Gospel tradition.

Institutional distribution and justification (‘bestowed… on the entire church’, catechumens/elect) explicitly applies the mysteries to church practice; even with ‘First Man/second man’ language, the paragraph’s function is ecclesial policy/interpretation.
